Honestly, at this pace it would be weeks, not days. My rough estimate is 2–4 weeks of continuous running.

| | |
|---|---|
| Main-owned open checks | 111 (the second session's 27 are separate) |
| Mix | Mostly browser and data proofs against V1, plus about 20 final acceptance checks |
| S001-B1 so far | About 3 hours and 60% done |
| Typical heavy browser check | 2–4 hours each |
| Faster checks | Provider checks (now theory-only) and accepting the second session's evidence: 15–45 minutes each |
| Total | About 150–300 hours of continuous work, run strictly one check at a time |

The estimate is uncertain because roughly one check in three uncovers a real Next defect or a V1 change, like Sub Jobs today. Those can double a check's time.

What would speed it up most:
1. **The server speed fix.** Job pages take 3–9 seconds to load, which causes random test timeouts and reruns. I'd expect it to cut 20–30% overall.
2. **Letting agents prepare the next check** while the current one runs, still closing them strictly in order. That removes most of the idle setup time between checks, probably 30–40%.
3. **Grouping neighbouring checks of the same kind,** such as list screens, into one test run where the order allows.

With all three, I'd expect roughly 1.5–2.5 weeks.
